cases.retrieval_goal: Explain why measurement noise is unwanted while a valid unusual outlier can be useful.

sources.label: Synthetic data-quality notes
sources.text: In these data-quality notes, noise means random measurement error. It is unwanted because it obscures the real signal. An outlier is an observation unusually far from the usual pattern. An outlier can be a valid measurement of a rare real event and can preserve useful information. A valid unusually high temperature may identify a heatwave; removing it merely because it is unusual can discard the event of interest.

required_answer_points: Noise is random measurement error in this stated context and obscures real signal.
A valid outlier may reflect a rare real event and preserve useful information.
Rarity alone does not justify discarding a valid outlier.

cases.retrieval_goal: Explain why being noisy and being an outlier do not imply one another.

sources.label: Synthetic overlap notes
sources.text: Here noise refers to measurement error, while outlier refers to an observation far from the usual pattern. A small measurement error can lie within the typical range and therefore need not be an outlier. An extreme observation can be a valid rare event and therefore need not be noise. A large erroneous measurement may be both noisy and an outlier. The categories can overlap, but neither category implies the other.

required_answer_points: A noisy measurement may lie in the usual range and need not be an outlier.
A valid extreme observation can be an outlier without being noise.
The categories may overlap, but neither implies the other.

cases.concept: measurement precision versus bias with numbers
cases.retrieval_goal: Compare precision and bias for two sensors using their stated means and standard deviations.

sources.label: Synthetic sensor experiment
sources.text: A reference interval is 100.0 ms. Sensor A has mean 104.0 ms and standard deviation 0.2 ms. Sensor B has mean 100.0 ms and standard deviation 2.0 ms. In this experiment, precision refers to repeatability and is assessed by standard deviation: smaller standard deviation means greater precision. Bias is mean minus the reference value. Sensor A is more precise but has +4.0 ms bias. Sensor B is less precise and has 0.0 ms bias for these stated means. Precision does not establish low bias.

required_answer_points: Smaller standard deviation indicates greater measurement precision here.
Sensor A is more precise, with +4.0 ms bias.
Sensor B is less precise, with 0.0 ms bias for the stated means.
Bias compares the mean with the 100.0 ms reference and is distinct from repeatability.

cases.retrieval_goal: Explain this min-max normalization formula and its range and fitting caveats.

sources.label: Synthetic preprocessing notes
sources.text: These notes use min-max normalization, not every meaning of normalization. For a nonconstant training range, x' = (x - min_train) / (max_train - min_train). Training values at min_train and max_train map to 0 and 1. Fit these extrema on the training data and reuse them on held-out data to avoid leaking held-out information into fitting. A later value outside the training range may map outside [0, 1]. A constant training range makes the displayed denominator zero and needs a separate policy; no such policy is specified here.

required_answer_points: The stated transform is min-max scaling using training extrema.
A nonconstant training range maps its minimum and maximum to 0 and 1.
Held-out values outside that training range can map outside [0, 1].
Training extrema are fitted only on training data and a constant range needs a separate policy.

cases.retrieval_goal: Distinguish classifier precision and recall and compute both for the stated screening example.

sources.label: Synthetic classification notes
sources.text: This binary screening example defines a positive as a detected disease case. The confusion matrix has TP = 30, FP = 10, and FN = 20. Classifier precision is TP / (TP + FP), the fraction of positive predictions that are true positives: 30 / 40 = 0.75 or 75%. Recall is TP / (TP + FN), the fraction of actual positive cases detected: 30 / 50 = 0.60 or 60%. Here classifier precision is a positive-prediction metric, not the standard-deviation notion of sensor precision. A false negative is a disease case missed by the classifier.

required_answer_points: Precision uses positive predictions as its denominator and equals 75%.
Recall uses actual positives as its denominator and equals 60%.
The terms refer to binary classification in this screening example.

cases.concept: BFS shortest paths and edge-weight limitation
cases.retrieval_goal: Explain why BFS finds shortest paths in an unweighted graph and the limitation with unequal weights.

sources.label: Synthetic graph notes
sources.text: Breadth-first search uses a FIFO queue and explores vertices in layers by number of edges from the start. In an unweighted graph, or when all edge costs are equal, this yields a path with the minimum number of edges and hence minimum total cost. With unequal edge weights, minimum edge count need not minimize total cost. In a graph with A->B cost 10, A->C cost 1, and C->B cost 1, BFS can select the one-edge A->B path although A->C->B has lower total cost 2.

required_answer_points: FIFO layer order explains the minimum-edge guarantee.
The cost guarantee applies to unweighted or equal-edge-cost graphs.
With unequal weights, a fewest-edge path can cost more than a longer path.

cases.retrieval_goal: Explain safe retries of the same logical request and conflict behavior when a key is reused with different input.

sources.label: Synthetic API contract
sources.text: This API stores an idempotency key, a canonical request hash, and the committed receipt atomically with the operation. Repeating the same key and identical canonical request returns the original committed receipt without applying effects again. Reusing that key with a different canonical request is a conflict and must not apply a second operation. A genuinely new logical operation needs a new key. If the server commits but the client times out before seeing the response, retrying the identical key and request recovers the receipt without duplicating the already committed effect.

required_answer_points: Same key plus identical canonical request replays the original receipt without duplicate effects.
Same key plus different canonical request conflicts rather than overwriting or applying again.
A timeout does not prove the operation was uncommitted; same-request retry can recover the receipt.
